title: Embedded Memory, Startup & the Build
relevance: Bare-metal interviews probe whether you understand how Flash/RAM, crt0, and the linker script make C globals valid before main—and where const, stack, and heap actually land.

phases.goal: Establish the on-chip memory map and that C does not start at main with globals already valid.

must_hit.point: Flash/ROM is non-volatile and holds compiled code, .rodata, and initial templates for initialized variables; RAM is volatile and holds .data, .bss, the stack, and the heap.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates Flash (survives power loss; code/constants/init images) from RAM (live workspace that is garbage after power-up).

must_hit.point: Peripherals are mapped into memory addresses; writing those addresses configures hardware.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions MMIO: timers/serial ports appear as addresses you write to configure.

must_hit.point: On reset, RAM holds random garbage, so jumping straight into main would leave initialized globals wrong and uninitialized arrays as noise.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses the idea that without startup copy/zero, values like an initialized global are not yet correct in RAM.

probes: Walk the Flash vs RAM vs peripherals map, then explain why a C program on a microcontroller cannot safely start at main immediately after reset.

hints.1: Think about what still exists after power loss versus what does not.
hints.2: Name the three regions, then say what would be wrong if the CPU entered main with untouched RAM.
hints.3: Flash: code/.rodata/init images; RAM: .data/.bss/stack/heap (volatile/garbage at power-up); peripherals at MMIO addresses—startup must fix globals before main.

phases.goal: Explain crt0 startup (.data copy, .bss zero), linker MEMORY/SECTIONS, VMA vs LMA, and the vector table handoff.

must_hit.point: After reset the CPU reads a hardcoded address for the initial stack pointer and Reset Handler; crt0 copies .data from Flash into RAM, zeroes .bss, then calls main.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Orders reset → SP/Reset Handler → copy initialized globals → zero .bss → main.

must_hit.point: .data holds explicitly non-zero static-duration variables (LMA in Flash, VMA in RAM); .bss holds zero-initialized statics; crt0 copies LMA→VMA for .data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties sections to storage duration rules and states LMA Flash / VMA RAM for .data.

must_hit.point: The linker script’s MEMORY and SECTIONS map merge object-file sections into chip regions and export boundary symbols (e.g. _sdata) that startup uses as copy bookmarks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes MEMORY regions, SECTIONS placement, and linker symbols consumed by Reset_Handler.

must_hit.point: VMA is the execution address; LMA is the permanent storage address—for .data, LMA is Flash and VMA is RAM.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines both terms and applies them specifically to .data.

must_hit.point: The vector table is an array of function pointers at a fixed address; earliest entries are initial SP and Reset Handler, forced to the start of FLASH via a section like .isr_vector.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links vector table placement to FLASH start and reset entry.

probes: What is the difference between VMA and LMA, and how do the Reset Handler and linker symbols use that for .data and .bss?

hints.1: Startup is a restaurant opening: unlock, arrange from the blueprint, wipe empty counters, then let customers in.
hints.2: Name SP + Reset Handler, then the .data copy and .bss zero using linker bookmarks; define VMA vs LMA for .data.
hints.3: crt0: copy Flash LMA→RAM VMA for .data, zero .bss via _sbss/_ebss-style symbols, then main; linker MEMORY/SECTIONS place .isr_vector at FLASH start.

phases.goal: Connect declaration site to Flash/RAM cost and argue static budgeting vs stack/heap collision risk.

must_hit.point: const goes in Flash (.rodata); initialized globals consume both Flash and RAM; zero-initialized globals use only RAM (.bss).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the three placements and stresses dual Flash+RAM cost for initialized globals.

must_hit.point: On bare metal, const lookup tables/string literals save RAM by keeping data exclusively in Flash.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says const is a physical RAM saver, not only type safety.

must_hit.point: Stack typically grows downward from high RAM while .data/.bss sit low; deep locals/recursion can silently overwrite globals (stack overflow)—prefer static allocation so budgets are compile-time proven.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes opposite growth directions, silent overwrite, and static allocation preference.

probes: Where do const, initialized globals, .bss, locals, and malloc land, and why do embedded systems prefer static allocation over deep stacks or a heap?

hints.1: Ask what each declaration costs in Flash versus RAM.
hints.2: Contrast .rodata-only const with .data’s dual residency, then stack-down vs globals-up collision.
hints.3: const→Flash only; initialized globals→Flash+RAM; .bss→RAM; stack down / heap up from end of .bss—static allocation proves limits at link/compile time.

phases.goal: Apply the build path—cross toolchain, objcopy image, printf retargeting, and Reset_Handler copy/zero loops.

must_hit.point: Cross-compilation uses a target-prefixed toolchain (e.g. arm-none-eabi-gcc), -mcpu for the ISA, -T for the linker script, then objcopy to produce a raw .bin/.hex to flash.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names host≠target, toolchain prefix, -mcpu, -T, and objcopy stripping to flashable image.

must_hit.point: Bare-metal printf needs retargeting (often implementing _write to a UART); without it, linking printf can pull huge I/O handlers that exhaust memory—audit with a .map file.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions newlib/_write UART retarget and .map as the size audit tool.

must_hit.point: Reset_Handler copies words from &_sidata to &_sdata until &_edata, then (separately) zeroes from &_sbss until &_ebss before main.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Sketches the Flash→RAM copy loop bounds and the .bss zero loop bounds from the worked examples.

probes: Trace int counter = 42 from linker script through Reset_Handler into RAM, then say what else you must implement for printf on bare metal.

hints.1: Follow one initialized global from LMA in Flash to VMA in RAM.
hints.2: Point at _sidata/_sdata/_edata for the copy, then _sbss/_ebss for zeroing; separately name _write/UART retarget.
hints.3: Linker sets .data > RAM AT > FLASH and LOADADDR; Reset_Handler copies then zeroes .bss; arm-none-eabi + -T + objcopy; retarget _write or printf bloats the image.

tradeoffs.topic: const (.rodata in Flash) vs initialized globals (.data)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: const stays only in Flash and saves RAM; initialized non-const globals keep an init image in Flash and a live copy in RAM, so they cost both.
Static globals make Flash/RAM needs visible at link time; deep stacks or malloc risk silent collision or runtime OOM, so bare metal prefers proven static budgets.

tradeoffs.topic: printf / newlib I/O vs retargeted lightweight path
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Unretargeted printf can pull massive generic handlers that blow the memory budget; implementing _write to UART (and checking the .map) keeps I/O sized for the chip.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a software soft reset that jumps straight to main reinitializes globals.
gotchas.correction: Without re-running crt0, .data and .bss keep stale values—bizarre bugs until copy/zero runs again.

gotchas.trap: Custom bootloader handoff or deep-sleep RAM power-down without re-init.
gotchas.correction: If RAM was not restored or startup was skipped, you must re-execute the initialization loop before trusting statics.

gotchas.trap: Code or data larger than MEMORY LENGTH.
gotchas.correction: The linker errors that a region overflowed; fix size or the LENGTH/layout, not runtime.

gotchas.trap: Linking printf without retargeting on bare metal.
gotchas.correction: Implement the low-level syscall (often _write to UART) or you pull huge I/O and exhaust Flash/RAM.

gotchas.trap: Huge locals or deep recursion on a downward-growing stack.
gotchas.correction: Stack can overwrite .data/.bss silently; prefer static allocation and keep stack depth bounded.
